If a patient experiences symptoms of neuropathy, such as pain, burning, tingling, numbness, or weakness, or if deficits in sensory modalities (light touch, pain, temperature, position sense, vibratory sensation) or motor strength are identified, treatment should be promptly reassessed to prevent the development of irreversible conditions. 2. Patients receiving ciprofloxacin (CIPRO) should be instructed to notify their healthcare provider immediately if they develop symptoms suggestive of neuropathy before continuing treatment. 3. In pediatric patients, musculoskeletal disorders, including joint-related adverse events, have been observed at a higher incidence compared to controls. Preclinical studies have shown that oral administration of ciprofloxacin caused lameness in immature dogs. 4. Histopathological examination of weight-bearing joints in these dogs revealed permanent cartilage lesions. Similarly, other quinolone-class drugs have been associated with cartilage erosions and arthropathy in immature animals across various species. 5. Ciprofloxacin and other fluoroquinolones have been linked to QT interval prolongation on electrocardiograms and, in rare cases, arrhythmias. Spontaneous reports of torsade de pointes have been documented during postmarketing surveillance in patients receiving fluoroquinolones, including ciprofloxacin. 6. Ciprofloxacin should be avoided in patients with known QT interval prolongation, risk factors for QT prolongation or torsade de pointes (e.g., congenital long QT syndrome, uncorrected electrolyte imbalances like hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia, or cardiac diseases such as heart failure, myocardial infarction, or bradycardia), and in those taking Class IA or Class III antiarrhythmic agents, tricyclic antidepressants, macrolides, or antipsychotics. 7. Elderly patients may be more susceptible to drug-induced effects on the QT interval. 8. Ciprofloxacin is an inhibitor of the hepatic CYP1A2 enzyme pathway. Co-administration of ciprofloxacin with drugs primarily metabolized by CYP1A2 (e.g., theophylline, methylxanthines, caffeine, tizanidine, ropinirole, clozapine, olanzapine) can lead to increased plasma concentrations of these drugs, potentially resulting in clinically significant pharmacodynamic side effects. 9. Ciprofloxacin has not been demonstrated to be effective in the treatment of syphilis. High-dose, short-term antimicrobial therapy for gonorrhea may mask or delay the symptoms of incubating syphilis. 10. All patients diagnosed with gonorrhea should undergo serologic testing for syphilis at the time of diagnosis and have a follow-up serologic test for syphilis three months after treatment with ciprofloxacin. 11. During clinical trials involving 49,038 patients treated with oral and parenteral ciprofloxacin, most adverse events were mild to moderate in severity, resolved shortly after discontinuation of the drug, and did not require additional treatment. 12. Ciprofloxacin was discontinued due to adverse events in 1% of orally treated patients. The most frequently reported drug-related adverse events across all formulations, dosages, durations, and indications were nausea (2.5%), diarrhea (1.6%), abnormal liver function tests (1.3%), vomiting (1%), and rash (1%). 13. Additional medically significant adverse events occurring in less than 1% of patients included headache, abdominal pain, foot pain, extremity pain, injection site reactions, palpitations, atrial flutter, syncope, hypertension, angina, myocardial infarction, restlessness, dizziness, insomnia, hallucinations, seizures, depression (including suicidal ideation or behavior), paresthesia, abnormal gait, oral candidiasis, gastrointestinal bleeding, hepatitis, renal failure, dyspnea, bronchospasm, allergic reactions, photosensitivity, blurred vision, tinnitus, and hearing loss. 14. In some cases, nausea, vomiting, tremor, irritability, or palpitations were attributed to elevated serum theophylline levels, likely due to drug interactions with ciprofloxacin. 15. Randomized, double-blind clinical trials comparing ciprofloxacin to cefuroxime axetil and clarithromycin in respiratory tract infections demonstrated a central nervous system (CNS) adverse event profile comparable to the control drugs. 16. In pediatric patients aged 1 to 17 years with complicated urinary tract infections or pyelonephritis, ciprofloxacin was compared to a cephalosporin in a study conducted across multiple countries. The primary objective was to assess musculoskeletal and neurological safety within six weeks of therapy and through one year of follow-up. 17. An Independent Pediatric Safety Committee reviewed all cases of musculoskeletal adverse events, including abnormal gait or joint examinations. These events were comprehensively evaluated and included conditions such as arthralgia, abnormal gait, joint sprains, leg pain, back pain, bone pain, myalgia, and decreased joint range of motion. 18. Affected joints included the knee, elbow, ankle, hip, wrist, and shoulder. Within six weeks of treatment initiation, the incidence of these events was 9.3% in the ciprofloxacin-treated group compared to 6% in the comparator group. Most events were mild or moderate in severity.
